intro: Introduction to European Union Law. Lecture four: competences, and how the Union legislates.

slides.4: The political groups in the Parliament after the 2024 election, given as a chart from the Parliament's own site.
slides.8: The sources of Union law again — the same hierarchy as before.
slides.14: A common mistake, and it is worth more than one exam mark: the catalogue is not the legal basis. The type of competence comes from the catalogue in Articles 2 to 6 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union — exclusive, under Articles 2, paragraph 1 and 3; shared, under Articles 2, paragraph 2 and 4; coordinating, supporting and supplementing, under Articles 2 paragraph 3, 2 paragraph 5, 5 and 6; plus the Common Foreign and Security Policy under Article 2, paragraph 4 of that Treaty and Articles 21 and following of the Treaty on European Union. The legal basis, by contrast, comes from the policy chapters. Article 2, paragraph 6 says so expressly: the scope of and arrangements for exercising the Union's competences are determined by the provisions of the Treaties relating to each area. So you cannot legislate on Article 3. You legislate on the article in the policy chapter, and the catalogue only tells you what kind of competence it is.
slides.22: Exercising a competence: two further tests. Having a competence is not enough; its exercise is controlled by two principles. Proportionality, Article 5, paragraph 4 of the Treaty on European Union, applies to all Union action. Subsidiarity, Article 5, paragraph 3, applies only where the competence is shared — and that restriction is a favourite trap: there is no subsidiarity test for exclusive competences.
slides.34: Two legislative procedures: the ordinary legislative procedure, and the special legislative procedure. And one note in the margin that matters: non-legislative acts follow different procedures again — see Article 289, paragraph 3. The ordinary procedure has been the usual one since the Treaty of Lisbon; which applies in a given case is determined by the legal basis, not by choice.
slides.36: The ordinary procedure, second reading. Parliament has three months to approve, reject or amend the Council's position, and the Council then accepts it or does not — in which case conciliation follows.
slides.40: Which reading, in practice. Take the stage at which acts were actually adopted, per legislative term, and the trend is dramatic. First-reading agreements rose from twenty-eight per cent in 1999 to 2004, to seventy-two per cent in 2004 to 2009, eighty-five per cent in 2009 to 2014, and eighty-nine per cent in 2014 to 2019 — while third-reading adoptions fell from twenty-two per cent to one per cent. In other words, the formal three-reading procedure has almost disappeared in practice. The reason comes next.
slides.41: Informal trilogues. Trilogues are informal negotiations between Parliament, Council and Commission that produce the agreement which the formal readings then rubber-stamp. They are the explanation for those figures. The standard criticism is transparency: the decisive bargaining happens outside the procedure the Treaties set out, in a format the Treaties do not mention.
slides.44: The consultation procedure, used in a limited set of policies: sensitive matters of police cooperation, emergency rules in asylum policy, tax policy, state aid, the system of own resources, and employment policy guidelines. The Council, usually acting unanimously, adopts the act on a Commission proposal after consulting Parliament — and now the crucial words: the Council must consult, but is not bound by Parliament's position. Failing to consult at all, however, is a procedural defect that annuls the act. The procedure has two faces: in fiscal matters it preserves intergovernmental features, while in foreign and defence policy it represents a step towards involving a Parliament previously not heard at all.
